papers.title: Long-term lead exposures and polygenic risk scores for iron load in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) has been linked to cumulative lead exposure. Iron is known to accumulate in the substantia nigra and may contribute to PD via oxidative stress and interactions with lead metabolism. OBJECTIVES: We assess whether effects of long-term lead exposures on PD are modified by iron-load polygenetic risk scores (PRSs). METHODS: We estimated tibia lead levels using DNA methylation biomarkers for 521 cases and 236 population controls from the Parkinson's Environment and Gene study, and created iron-load PRSs (transferrin saturation [TSAT], ferritin, serum iron and total iron binding capacity) based on iron-homeostasis related single-nucleotide polymorphisms from previous studies. We estimated effects of lead on PD stratified by percentiles of TSAT and ferritin PRS using logistic regressions. We conducted stratified analyses by gender. RESULTS: Estimated tibia lead effects on PD were increased at the lowest (1st quintile) TSAT PRS (odds ratio [OR] = 1.79 [1.13-2.96]), while no associations were observed at higher TSAT PRS quintiles; furthermore, these associations were restricted to women (1st quintile: OR = 2.91 [1.33-7.63]) for whom we also estimated a statistically significant trend across TSAT PRS levels. We also observed tibia lead associations on PD in the lowest and two highest quartiles of the ferritin PRS, but these associations were not formally statistically significant. CONCLUSIONS: Genetic susceptibility to iron deficiency in general may increase associations between cumulative lead exposure and PD with strong effect modification observed among women for iron load. This suggests that iron load or iron transport mechanisms may play a protective role against neurotoxicity of lead among women.

papers.title: Serum neurofilament light chain and striatal specific binding ratio predict motor and cognitive outcomes in tremor dominant versus postural instability/gait difficulty subtypes of Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) exhibits clinical heterogeneity between tremor-dominant (TD) and postural instability/gait difficulty (PIGD) subtypes. Whether striatal dopaminergic denervation mediates associations between serum neurofilament light chain (NfL), a marker of neuroaxonal injury, and disease progression remains unclear. METHODS: We analyzed 264 patients with de novo PD (TD, n = 177; PIGD, n = 80) and 132 healthy controls (HCs) from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI). Baseline NfL and dopamine transporter (DAT) single-photon emission computed tomography-derived striatal specific binding ratios (SBRs) were assessed. Spearman correlations, linear mixed-effects models, and mediation analyses examined cross-sectional relationships, five-year clinical outcomes, and mediation. RESULTS: Serum NfL was higher in PD than in controls (P = 0.002), without significant subtype differences (P = 0.661). Higher NfL correlated with worse motor and cognitive function and lower caudate SBR (r = -0.270, P < 0.001). Baseline NfL predicted five-year motor deterioration (MDS-UPDRS III: β = 0.239, P = 0.043) and cognitive decline (MoCA: β = -0.063, P = 0.037). Subtype analyses associated NfL with cognitive decline in TD (β = -0.076, P = 0.031) and motor deterioration in PIGD (β = 0.564, P = 0.004). Caudate, anterior caudate, and posterior caudate SBRs significantly mediated associations with both outcomes (indirect effects, P < 0.05). CONCLUSIONS: Baseline serum NfL predicts five-year deterioration with subtype-specific patterns. Caudate SBRs partially mediate these associations, while residual cognitive associations suggest possible extrastriatal involvement. papers.title: Cancer Incidence After Parkinson Disease: A Nationwide Multi-Cohort Study With Genetic Analyses.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Epidemiologic studies suggest altered cancer susceptibility in Parkinson disease (PD), but the magnitude and biological basis of these associations remain unclear. We aimed to quantify cancer risk after PD diagnosis, identify cancer-specific patterns, and evaluate contributions of smoking and shared genetic mechanisms. METHODS: This retrospective study integrated 3 Finnish cohorts: biobank-based FinnGen, nationwide register-based FINPARK, and the clinically validated Turku University Hospital cohort. PD cases were matched to controls by age and sex, and analyses included cancers diagnosed after the index date. Fine-Gray competing-risk and Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) of incident cancer. Genetic analyses included Mendelian randomization (MR), linkage disequilibrium score regression (LDSC), polygenic risk score (PGS), and genome-wide association studies (GWAS). RESULTS: The FinnGen, FINPARK, and Turku cohorts included 4,277 individuals with PD (42,770 matched controls), 21,105 (63,285), and 1,103 (1,103), respectively. Across cohorts (mean age at PD diagnosis, 68.7-70.8 years; 40%-46% female), PD was associated with a 31%-41% lower overall cancer risk (Fine-Gray HR range 0.59 [95% CI 0.55-0.65] to 0.69 [0.66-0.72]). The strongest reductions were observed for respiratory (HR range 0.11-0.42) and gastrointestinal cancers (HR range 0.37-0.64). These associations persisted in Cox and smoking-adjusted analyses. Genetic analyses used FinnGen (n = 520,210) and previous European GWAS meta-analyses. MR estimates were consistent with inverse associations between PD genetic liability and respiratory (OR 0.943 [0.900-0.985]), gastrointestinal (0.966 [0.932-0.999]), and skin cancers (0.967 [0.943-0.991]). papers.title: MobilityAPP: A Randomized Controlled Trial Evaluating Gait-Focused Physiotherapy in Parkinson Disease and Atypical Parkinsonian Syndromes.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Physiotherapy is a crucial element of care strategies for parkinsonian syndromes, especially in atypical parkinsonian disorders (APDs), where levodopa response is limited. Preliminary studies in APDs have reported improvements in walking and motor functions; however, small sample sizes represented a common limitation because of the rare nature of these diseases. The Mobility in Atypical Parkinsonism: a Trial of Physiotherapy (MobilityAPP) aims to investigate the superiority of gait-focused physiotherapy (GPT) in improving self-paced gait speed, compared with standard physiotherapy (SPT). METHODS: This double-blind, randomized controlled trial was conducted in 5 centers across Europe. Patients with multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy, and Parkinson disease (PD) were recruited through outpatient clinics or from specialized wards. Patients were included if they had a Hoehn and Yahr stage below 4 and excluded if their medication had been adapted recently or ambulation was influenced by other preconditions. After a 1-week home monitoring of physical activity, participants were randomized (1:1) to inpatient GPT or SPT for 2 weeks, followed by 5 weeks of home-based training. The primary outcome was the pre-post change in self-paced gait speed, measured with wearable sensors during a standardized 2 × 10-m walking test. Secondary outcomes included clinical scores, patient-reported outcomes (PROMs), and digital mobility measures from daily life. Repeated-measures analysis of variance was used to assess primary and secondary outcomes. RESULTS: Of 167 patients screened, 160 were included (mean age 67.4, 51.2% female) and 151 completed the study per protocol (85 with APD, 66 with PD; 76 GPT, 75 SPT). papers.title: Levodopa-responsive parkinsonism with dystonia in RAB39B-related Waisman syndrome: a case report.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pathogenic variants in RAB39B, located on chromosome Xq28, cause a rare X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by intellectual disability and early-onset parkinsonism, commonly referred to as Waisman syndrome. RAB39B encodes a neuron-specific small GTPase involved in vesicular trafficking and synaptic regulation. Increasing evidence suggests that RAB39B deficiency produces a clinical continuum spanning neurodevelopmental impairment and later neurodegeneration. While parkinsonism is the most consistently reported motor manifestation, the spectrum of associated movement disorders remains incompletely defined, and cranial dystonia has been rarely characterized. We report a case of genetically confirmed RAB39B-related disease presenting with levodopa-responsive parkinsonism associated with multifocal dystonia, including upper-limb dystonia and mixed oromandibular dystonia. CASE PRESENTATION: A 48-year-old right-handed man with longstanding intellectual disability presented with an eight-year history of progressive extrapyramidal symptoms beginning with a resting tremor of the right upper limb. Over time he developed bradykinesia, rigidity, freezing of gait, and oromandibular dystonia. Childhood history was notable for developmental delay and longstanding dystonic posturing of the digits. Family history revealed similar neurological features in a younger brother and dystonic toe posturing in the mother, suggesting X-linked inheritance. Neurological examination demonstrated hypomimia, slow saccades, tongue bradykinesia, mixed oromandibular dystonia, generalized rigidity with right-predominant resting tremor, and dystonic digital posturing. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed susceptibility changes involving the bilateral globus pallidi, substantia nigra, and posterior thalami. papers.title: Chaperone-mediated autophagy targets Miro-1 for degradation to promote mitophagy and inhibit α-synuclein induced ferroptosis.
papers.abstract: Ferroptotic neurodegeneration has emerged as a key pathological driver in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the upstream mechanisms that connect α-synuclein pathology to ferroptosis remain poorly defined. To delineate how pathological α-synuclein triggers mitochondria-associated ferroptosis via chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) inhibition, and to develop targeted approaches for intervening in ferroptotic neurodegeneration. α-Synuclein pathology was modeled using pre-formed fibrils (PFFs) in differentiated SH-SY5Y cells and A53T transgenic mice. Ferroptosis, mitophagy and CMA were assessed using biochemical, imaging and genetic approaches. A midbrain-targeted acoustically activatable liposomal formulation loaded with the CMA agonist CA77.1 (AAL-CA) was engineered to achieve site-specific CMA activation in vivo. We found that α-synuclein pathology induced ferroptosis and impaired mitophagy in PD models. Mechanistically, α-synuclein stress suppressed CMA activity, resulting in Miro-1 accumulation by impairing its degradation. Accumulated Miro-1 competed with PINK1 for binding to TOMM70, thereby inhibiting PINK1-Parkin-mediated mitophagy. Genetic manipulation of Miro-1 levels, combined with pharmacological modulation of CMA, demonstrated that Miro-1 accumulation is both sufficient and necessary to inhibit mitophagy and ferroptosis under α-synuclein stress. Midbrain-targeted AAL-CA activated CMA, reduced Miro-1 levels, restored mitophagy, inhibited ferroptosis, preserved dopaminergic neurons, and improved motor deficits in A53T mice. Collectively, CMA dysfunction links α-synuclein pathology to ferroptosis via Miro-1-dependent mitophagy impairment. Targeted CMA activation is a promising disease-modifying approach for PD.

papers.title: Six Years after the Storm: Drawing the First Line on COVID-19 and Parkinson's Disease.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: Six years after the SARS-CoV-2 outbreak, we revisit the fear of a post-COVID parkinsonism wave, echoing encephalitis lethargica after the 1918 pandemic, through two questions. First, is the infection a risk factor for de novo Parkinson's disease (PD)? Epidemiology reveals no robust signal, yet pathological, imaging, and experimental evidence shows the virus targets the olfactory-brainstem axis, sustains neuroinflammation, promotes α-synuclein aggregation, and leaves a dopaminergic footprint. We hypothesize an inflammation-driven, rather than directly cytopathic, mechanism in vulnerable individuals, with persistent post-COVID hyposmia as a candidate risk marker. As the PD prodrome outlasts available follow-up, this question remains open. Second, does infection alter the trajectory of established PD? Motor and non-motor worsening during and shortly after COVID-19 is consistently demonstrated. However, accelerated neurodegeneration remains unproven. Neither alarm nor reassurance is warranted, but long-term, prospective, harmonized cohorts enriched for hyposmia and characterized with α-synuclein seed amplification assays, neurofilament light chain, and dopamine transporter imaging are needed. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

papers.title: Digital Biomarker of Upper-Limb Bradykinesia Severity, Progression, and Therapy Response in Parkinson's Disease.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Bradykinesia is central to diagnosing and monitoring Parkinson's disease (PD). Its severity is measured with ordinal clinical scales that require an expert, compress distinct motor features into one number, and show ceiling and floor effects. OBJECTIVES: To develop and validate the Digital Bradykinesia Composite Score (DBCS), a measure of upper-limb bradykinesia derived from ordinary finger-tapping videos. METHODS: We analyzed 3020 finger tapping videos from 656 participants (379 PD, 155 atypical parkinsonism, 33 rapid eye movement [REM] sleep behavior disorder, 79 controls, 10 other diagnoses) recorded at more than 20 sites. Computer vision extracted kinematic features, which were combined into four domains (vigor, reflecting tapping speed and amplitude; timing; irregularity; sequence effect) and the DBCS. We evaluated the DBCS against clinician ratings, levodopa and deep brain stimulation (DBS), dopamine transporter (DaT) imaging, substantia nigra free water, and 24 weeks of unsupervised home recordings. RESULTS: The DBCS increased with clinical severity. It improved with levodopa and with DBS, with responsiveness similar to that of the clinical rating. In patients with DBS, levodopa was associated with a further improvement in the DBCS but not in the clinical rating. Over 24 weeks of home recordings, the DBCS increased in patients and decreased slightly in controls. Higher scores were associated with lower striatal DaT binding and higher nigral free water. CONCLUSIONS: A composite score derived from ordinary video was associated with bradykinesia severity, treatment response, 6-month change, and markers of nigrostriatal degeneration, which supports its further evaluation for remote monitoring and as an endpoint in clinical trials. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

papers.title: Translational neuroscience in psychoeducation: Mapping non-motor circuitry to clinical management in movement disorders.
papers.abstract: Non-motor symptoms (NMS) affect nearly all patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) and related movement disorders, with a mean of roughly 8-10 discrete symptoms per individual. Their effect on quality of life often exceeds that of motor features, yet NMS remain under-recognized and undertreated, partly because patients and caregivers lack a working model of why these symptoms arise in a "movement" disease. This chapter applies neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) to that gap and positions it relative to conventional psychoeducation, health communication, and behavioral science. We propose the Map-Normalize-Differentiate-Navigate (MNDN) workflow as a movement-disorders-specific implementation of the NIPE framework described in Chapter 1 of this volume. MNDN is a clinical proposal, not a validated protocol: its components are specified so that it can be tested, but its effects on patient outcomes have not been evaluated. Drawing on the tripartite cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loop model and multi-transmitter degeneration, we provide modules for seven high-yield NMS: apathy, anxiety, executive dysfunction, REM sleep behavior disorder, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, psychosis, and fatigue. Each module summarizes the neural systems implicated, at the level of certainty the evidence supports, together with common misattributions, reversible contributors that must be excluded, management options and their limits, and patient and caregiver handout content. We describe delivery formats from 3 to 5 min "micro-NIPE" sessions in routine visits to group and telehealth programs, specify the minimum components, provider competencies, dose, fidelity criteria, and proximal outcomes needed to test MNDN, and examine the ethical risks of neurobiological framing (determinism, oversimplification, over-attribution, and false reassurance), with particular attention to prognostic counseling in REM sleep behavior disorder. papers.title: The effect of music therapy on function in people with Parkinson's disease or parkinsonism: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveThe investigation intended to assess the effects of music therapy on functional impairments in individuals with Parkinson's disease or parkinsonism.MethodsFrom inception to 31 August 2026, the following databases were searched systematically and independently by two investigators, including China National Knowledge Infrastructure, VIP, Wanfang Data, SinoMed, PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Scopus, concerning music therapy for Parkinson's disease or parkinsonism. The publication bias risk was determined using funnel plots and Egger's regression test.ResultsThirty-three studies of generally good quality were included, involving 3635 patients. papers.title: Impact of Foslevodopa/Foscarbidopa on Key Clinical and Patient-Reported Outcomes in Patients With Advanced Parkinson's Disease: Responder Analysis of Two Phase 3 Clinical Trials.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: A post hoc responder analysis was conducted to evaluate the impact of foslevodopa/foscarbidopa (LDp/CDp) on achieving meaningful responses in clinical and patient reported outcomes among people with advanced Parkinson's disease (PwaP). METHODS: Data from two trials evaluating 24-h/day continuous subcutaneous LDp/CDp infusion in PwaP were included: (1) a 12-week, randomized, double-blind, phase 3 trial (ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT04380142) and (2) a 52-week, open-label, multicenter study (NCT03781167). Responders were identified relative to baseline for increased "On" time without troublesome dyskinesia (ONwoTD) and reduced "Off" time using ≥ 1-h and ≥ 3-h thresholds (robust responder). Established minimal clinically important differences evaluated Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale Part II (MDS-UPDRS-II), Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire-39 (PDQ-39), European Quality of Life 5-Dimensions 5-Level (EQ-5D-5L), and Parkinson's Disease Sleep Scale-2 (PDSS-2) responders. Adjusted generalized linear models compared responder proportions treated with LDp/CDp versus oral levodopa/carbidopa (LD/CD) at weeks 4 and 12, and outcomes through week 52. RESULTS: By week 12, a greater percentage of patients on LDp/CDp versus those on oral LD/CD experienced statistically significant (*P < 0.05) outcome improvements with 82.7%* versus 50.2% achieving 1-h reductions in "Off" time and 61.2%* versus 27.8% achieving ≥ 3-h reductions. Similarly, 83.1%* versus 48.3% of patients achieved ≥ 1-h increases in ONwoTD and 63.4%* versus 26.1% achieved ≥ 3-h increases. A greater proportion of patients on LDp/CDp achieved complete (100%) "Off" time resolution (42.7%* vs 14.4%), as well as reduced MDS-UPDRS-II (46.6%* vs 21.9%) and PDSS-2 scores (68.6%* vs 45.4%). papers.title: Association between caregiver roles, nocturnal care and agitation in home-dwelling patients with Alzheimer's disease, dementia with Lewy body, and Parkinson's disease dementia.
papers.abstract: BackgroundAgitation is a common and disabling neuropsychiatric symptom among dementia patients, predominantly occurs during nighttime, and brings heavy burden on caregivers.ObjectiveTo analyze the association between agitation and caregiver related factors in home dwelling patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD).MethodsThis cross-sectional study enrolled 69 home-dwelling AD patients, 44 DLB patients, and 25 PDD patients between January and December 2024. papers.title: LRRK2 Negatively Regulates BDNF/TrkB Signaling and Neurovascular Function After Cerebral Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury.
papers.journal: FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology
papers.abstract: Gain-of-function mutations of leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) are neurotoxic, cause Parkinson's disease, and associate with risk of ischemic stroke. We explored the role of LRRK2 in transient oxygen/glucose deprivation (tOGD)-induced HUVEC and HT-22 neuronal cells, and after transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) in rats. tOGD increased LRRK2 protein and suppressed BDNF, Notch signaling, CD31, capillary-like network formation, and cellular viability in HUVEC. These suppressions were blocked by LRRK2 siRNA or the LRRK2 inhibitor MLi-2. HSC70-dependent chaperone-mediated autophagy can clear LRRK2. Using the HSC70 activator salidroside, HSC70 siRNA, and the HSC70 inhibitor Ver155008, we showed that the tOGD-dependent increases in LRRK2 and their effects were reversed by activating HSC70. The TrkB inhibitor ANA-12 and the Notch inhibitor DAPT both blocked the salidroside-dependent activation of Notch after tOGD, although DAPT did not prevent salidroside-induced increases in BDNF. Similarly, tOGD increased LRRK2 protein in HT-22 cells, and LRRK2-dependent reductions in BDNF and neuronal differentiation were prevented by salidroside via an HSC70-dependent mechanism.
